messages.subject: Comparing nested models that include random slopes
messages.subject_clean: Comparing nested models that include random slopes
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have a question about comparing nested models that include random slopes.
We're interested in the effect of an IV and want to include random slopes
in the models (to "keep it maximal"). The full model is:

     model1 <- lmer(DV ~ IV + (1|subject) + (1+IV|item), data=data)

I want to compare model1 to a reduced model using a likelihood ratio test
to determine whether the model that includes IV provides a better fit of
the data than one without IV. I'm unclear which of the following I should
use for the base model:

     model2 <- lmer(DV ~ (1|subject) + (1|item), data=data)
     model3 <- lmer(DV ~ (1|subject) + (1+IV|item), data=data)

It seems like model2 isn't appropriate because then model1 and model2
differ in two ways (the fixed effect of IV and the random by-item slopes
for IV), so that doesn't tell us about the effect of IV as a fixed effect
alone. That is if anova(model2,model1) is significant, it might be because
of the random by-item slope for IV and not the fixed effect of IV.

In model3, it seems strange to include a random slope for a variable that
isn't included as a fixed effect. But, at least then only one thing differs
between the two models.

We could just look at the summary output for model 1, but because the IV
has three levels, it will only return pairwise comparisons between the
three levels and not information equivalent to a "main effect" for the IV.

Many thanks for any help you can offer!
Best,
Julia

--

That is if anova(model2,model1) is significant, it might be because of the random by-item slope for IV and not the fixed effect of IV.
>

Dear Julia,

You are correct: The comparison between model1 and model3 is exactly what the logic of Barr et al. 2013 implies for this situation.  You are right that model3 on its own would in most cases be odd to posit as an a-priori plausibly “correct” model underlying your data.  However, if your IV is within-items and between-subjects, then model3 is exactly the right model to use as a baseline against which to perform an omnibus test of the contribution of the fixed effects of IV, given the possibility that the effects of the various levels of IV vary among items.  So, if the omnibus test (the overall “main effect” of a 3-level factor) is the one you want to do, then the comparison between model1 and model3 is the one that will give it to you.

Best

Roger
